research_text:
## 1. API and finding

`PBEKeySpec` represents password material and, in two of its constructors, parameters for deriving a password-based key. The **second argument is `byte[] salt`**; the iteration count is the third. The four-argument constructor also takes a requested key length. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/spec/PBEKeySpec.html))

The detector message concerns the salt’s randomized-source property, not the iteration count. The supplied CrySL file requires `randomized[salt]`. It does not define how a detector proves that predicate or map detector error names to predicates. The supplied metadata’s separate claim about an iteration count below 10,000 therefore cannot be substituted for an explanation of the salt message; resolving that discrepancy requires review. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/PBEKeySpec.crysl))

## 2. Documented usage and remediation guidance

- Oracle documents nonempty, non-null salt and positive iteration count for both salt-taking constructors; the four-argument constructor also requires a positive key length. These are API validity checks, not a guarantee that the parameters meet a security policy. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/spec/PBEKeySpec.html))
- For newly generated PBE parameters, Oracle’s guide illustrates generating salt with `SecureRandom`. RFC 8018 discusses random salt selection and, for uses where keys may interact, salt that also distinguishes operations. `SecureRandom.nextBytes` fills an array with random bytes. These are general usage recommendations, not a finding-specific fix. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/security/java-cryptography-architecture-jca-reference-guide.html))
- Oracle recommends password `char[]` values rather than immutable strings. `clearPassword()` clears the spec’s internal copy; callers must also clear password copies they retain or obtain from `getPassword()`. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/spec/PBEKeySpec.html))
- The CrySL file sets `iterationCount >= 10000`; that is **the rule’s threshold**, not a minimum stated by the `PBEKeySpec` constructor documentation. The API documentation does not provide a universal remediation procedure or establish that changing a particular call alone is sufficient. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/PBEKeySpec.crysl))

## 3. Compatibility and migration

- **Existing encrypted data:** Oracle states that decryption needs the same PBE salt and iteration count used for encryption. Its guide describes retrieving encoded cipher parameters for later use. Thus, replacing historical parameters with newly generated ones is not equivalent when reading existing data. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/security/java-cryptography-architecture-jca-reference-guide.html))
- **Stored password verifiers:** For its password-verifier scope, NIST says to store each salt and hash and recommends storing the scheme and cost factor to enable migration. This is guidance for that use case, not a format or automatic migration facility specified by `PBEKeySpec`. ([pages.nist.gov](https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b.html?utm_source=openai))
- **Wire or persisted formats:** RFC 8018 defines an optional standardized PBKDF2 parameter structure containing the salt, iteration count, optional key length, and PRF. `PBEKeySpec` itself does not prescribe an application’s persisted or wire format. ([datatracker.ietf.org](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8018))
- **Platforms:** Oracle documents `PBEKeySpec` since Java 1.4; Android documents the class and its constructors from API level 1. Availability of a particular algorithm and provider is a separate compatibility question. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/spec/PBEKeySpec.html))

The reviewed API sources do not specify a universal migration path for an application’s existing data or protocol. Those formats, algorithms, providers, and peer requirements remain unresolved.

## 4. Exact supplied rule

The supplied file declares the governed type, events, and salt requirement as follows: ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/PBEKeySpec.crysl))

```text
SPEC javax.crypto.spec.PBEKeySpec

c1: PBEKeySpec(password, salt, iterationCount, keyLength);
cp1: clearPassword();

randomized[salt];
```

Its object declarations type the four event arguments as `char[]`, `byte[]`, `int`, and `int`. Thus, the declared construction event has a **four-argument parameter list**; the declared `clearPassword` event has no arguments. Both are declared under `SPEC javax.crypto.spec.PBEKeySpec`. The file also lists the one- and three-argument constructors as forbidden, orders construction before clearing, and separately constrains the iteration count and password. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/PBEKeySpec.crysl))

**No: the rule as declared is not a name-only rule for an unrelated method that merely shares one of those names.** The file scopes its events to `javax.crypto.spec.PBEKeySpec` and declares their argument lists. It does not, by itself, specify the detector’s implementation or prove how a particular detector version resolves calls. The supplied SHA-256 was not independently verified against an immutable rule revision; the provided URL points to the mutable `master` branch. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/PBEKeySpec.crysl))
